docs.title: Welcome!
docs.text: This is an updated 100% free & ad-free embedded systems development course focusing on the ESP32 and the native ESP-IDF framework. Learn at your own pace, with zero distractions!

docs.title: What makes this different
docs.text: Unlike older courses, it focuses on the fundamentals, AI-integrated workflows, and what AI still struggles with. Plus, every single concept is taught through projects. You learn by doing, not reading, right from the first chapter!

docs.title: We skip over
docs.text:
• memorizing syntax and API
  • typing code manually

docs.title: We focus on
docs.text:
• learning the fundamentals
  • writing code using AI efficiently
  • reviewing what the AI generates

docs.title: Why ESP32
docs.text: ESP32 microcontrollers are cheap, and comes with WiFi and Bluetooth bulit-in. Extremely useful for IoT products.

docs.title: Why ESP-IDF Over Arduino Core
docs.text: Since the purpose of this course is to learn embedded systems, using a low level framework like ESP-IDF is benefitial as it exposes many details that Arduino Core abstracts away. ESP-IDF is designed for commercial-grade products rather than simple hobby prototypes.

docs.title: Is this course AI-generated?
docs.text: No. Click here to learn why this is not AI-generated, this course was made, and what it prioritizes.

docs.title: Current state of the course
docs.text: This course is heavily in development. Feel free to contibute.

docs.title: Why isn't this course AI-generated?
docs.text:
I previously created an embedded C course using AI, but I deleted it due to the following issues:

  • It assumed knowledge that was only introduced in later chapters.
  • Instead of breaking concepts down into smaller pieces, it introduced large amounts of new material all at once.
  • It contained inaccurate details regarding tool configurations and setup instructions (which change frequently).
  • It was not project-based.
  • It lacked screenshots and visual aids.

This course is designed to fix those problems.

docs.title: No disruptions
docs.text:
I will ensure that you never have to stop and wonder, "What does that mean?" while reading.

Unlike a documentation, this is an opinionated course, meant to be read from top to bottom, from the first chapter to the last chapter. Everything is explained either immediately as you read, or beforehand. Meaning you shouldn't need to scroll down a bit to check for the explanation, and scroll back up. But feel free to skip things you already know.

If I skip an explanation that isn't immediately relevant (such as legacy configurations that exist purely for backward compatibility), I will let you know upfront. For example, "This value exists for legacy purposes, so we don't need to worry about it."

docs.title: No overwhelm
docs.text:
Rather than presenting code first and explaining it afterward (the typical AI approach), I will build your mental model first and define key terminology before introducing the code, allowing you to grasp it immediately.

Instead of dropping large code snippets, I will show you:

  1. The simplest, shortest code to achieve the functional goal first.
  2. Step-by-step improvements from there.

I will do my best to avoid overwhelming you.

docs.title: Does that mean I don't use AI at all?
docs.text:
No. I still use AI for:

  • Double-checking factual accuracy.
  • Learning complex topics so I can explain them clearly.
  • Polishing grammar and flow for certain sentences or paragraph only.
  • Creating the initial draft (only occasionally).
  • Generating code

Now, click here to return to the homepage.

docs.title: Blinking an LED
docs.text:
Let's have a look at our ESP32 microcontroller:

As you can see, there are a lot of pins underneath it. These are called GPIO pins (General Purpose Input Output pins). These pins are the primary way in which the ESP32 control external hardware. Each pin can be turned HIGH voltage or LOW voltage.

Note

All of those pins are not GPIO pins, but the majority are. You will discover other pins (like GND) later in the course.

What we are going to now is to make the GPIO22 pin HIGH and LOW continuously (like it's blinking), and connect an LED to that pin so it will turn ON and OFF. No need to worry about why we chose GPIO22 for now.

docs.title: Create a new empty project
docs.text: Create a new empty project using the sample_project template. We covered it in this chapter: Your First Project. Name it led_blink.

docs.title: Initialize Git
docs.text: Run git init to initialize the repository. Commit the changes with the commit message "initial commit" and optionally push to GitHub.

docs.title: Write the code
docs.text:
The code is self-explanatory:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"

void app_main(void)
{
    // Clean up previous configuration in GPIO22
    gpio_reset_pin(GPIO_NUM_22);

    // Configure GPIO22 for voltage output
    gpio_set_direction(GPIO_NUM_22, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    ESP_LOGI("MAIN", "Starting LED...");

    while (1) {
        // Set output voltage (1 means HIGH voltage)
        gpio_set_level(GPIO_NUM_22, 1);
        ESP_LOGI("MAIN", "LED State: ON");

        // Wait 1000 milliseconds (1 second)
        // pdMS_TO_TICKS() convert milliseconds to ticks (more on that later)
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));

        // 0 means LOW voltage
        gpio_set_level(GPIO_NUM_22, 0);
        ESP_LOGI("MAIN", "LED State: OFF");

        // Wait for 1 second (again)
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));
    }
}

Here, pdMS_TO_TICKS is a function-like macro that converts milliseconds to ticks. vTaskDelay only accepts ticks. If you do not know about macros, learn it right now by asking an AI. It's something that we use regularly.

You can commit the changes to your repository now.

docs.title: Improving the code
docs.text:
GPIO_NUM22 and the TAG are used in multiple parts of the code. It's better to define them in the top of the file, rather than repeating each time:

#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include <stdio.h>

// object-like macro to define the GPIO to be blinked
#define BLINK_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

// used for logging
static const char *TAG = "MAIN";

void app_main(void) {
  gpio_reset_pin(BLINK_GPIO);
  gpio_set_direction(BLINK_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

  ESP_LOGI(TAG, "Starting LED...");

  while (1) {
    gpio_set_level(BLINK_GPIO, 1);
    ESP_LOGI(TAG, "LED State: ON");
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));

    gpio_set_level(BLINK_GPIO, 0);
    ESP_LOGI(TAG, "LED State: OFF");
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));
  }
}

Commit these changes with a proper commit message.

How to build the project

Run the ESP-IDF: Build Your Project command from the command palette.

How to flash the project

Refer to the following section: Your First Project - Flashing

docs.title: Connect your LED
docs.text:
Now, your GPIO22 pin must be turning ON and OFF repeatedly. But we can't see it yet. Time to set up the circuit:

  • Connect the positive terminal of your LED to GPIO22 (labelled as D22).
  • Connect the negative terminal of your LED to a 220 Ω to 330 Ω resistor (this is important; without a resistor, you might damage your microcontroller).
  • Connect the other end of the resistor to the GND pin (ground pin) in the ESP32.

Now, you should see your LED blinking. Congrats!

docs.title: Hardware interrupts
docs.text:
Draft

This chapter is not completed yet.

In this chapter, we are going to write a program which allows us to toggle an LED using a button (we don't need a real button, we'll use a workaround!).

The connections are the same as before (LED & resistor). But we have to connect a jumper wire to GPIO23. Leave the other end of the jumper wire not connected to anything. Touching the other end of this jumper wire to the GND pin in the ESP32 will toggle the LED (equivalent to what happens internally when we press a real button).

docs.title: ISR handler
docs.text: ISR handler stands for Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) handler. It's a function that we configure to be run immediately when a hardware event occurs (in this case, the button press).

docs.title: IRAM_ATTR
docs.text:
While creating ISRs, we prefix IRAM_ATTR before the function name:

static void IRAM_ATTR my_isr_handler(void* arg)
{
    // code to toggle the LED
}

IRAM_ATTR is a preprocessor macro that makes this function load directly into internal instruction RAM (IRAM), instead of running them from the external flash memory. This makes the loading much faster.

But aren't functions already stored in RAM?

On most standard computers, all programs and functions are fully loaded in to the RAM before they run, but not in ESP32.

ESP32 (and other MCUs) have very limited RAM (less than 1 MB). So, functions remain in the external Flash memory chip and are read on the fly through a small cache.

docs.title: How we are going to do this (conceptually)
docs.text:
• We set the button GPIO pin to input mode, which will allow the ESP32 to read the voltage in the button pin.
  • We give a constant HIGH voltage to the button pin.
  • We put a resistor (also called pull-up resistor) between the voltage source and the pin, allowing us to connect the pin to GND (zero voltage) without causing high current.
  • We configure the button pin to trigger a signal (interrupt) when it goes from HIGH to LOW.
  • Now, when we touch the other end of the wire to GND, the voltage of the button pin will drop to LOW, triggering the interrupt, and causing the ISR handler to execute.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"

#define BUTTON_PIN GPIO_NUM_23
#define LED_PIN    GPIO_NUM_2

static int led_state = 0;

static void IRAM_ATTR gpio_isr_handler(void* arg) {
    led_state = !led_state;
    gpio_set_level(LED_PIN, led_state);
}

void app_main(void) {
    // Configure LED pin
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_PIN);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_PIN, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    // Configure Button pin with internal pull-up and falling edge interrupt
    gpio_reset_pin(BUTTON_PIN);
    gpio_set_direction(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_MODE_INPUT);
    gpio_set_pull_mode(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_PULLUP_ONLY);
    gpio_set_intr_type(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_INTR_NEGEDGE);

    // Install GPIO ISR service and add the handler
    gpio_install_isr_service(0);
    gpio_isr_handler_add(BUTTON_PIN, gpio_isr_handler, NULL);

    while (1) {
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));
    }
}

docs.title: Test the code
docs.text:
Now, after building and flashing, touch the button pin to GND. If you did everything correctly, the LED will respond to the input.

Now that the code has been tested, you can commit and push your changes.

docs.title: Improving the code
docs.text:
Currently, we are toggling the LED directly inside the ISR handler. This isn't recommended because ISR handlers have very high priority and they will block other running tasks. ISR handlers are kept minimal.

So, we do this:

  • ISR handler doesn't toggle the LED directly, it adds an item to a queue
  • We run a task that constantly waits for items in the queue to process it
  • When a new item get added to the queue, the task consumes it, and toggles the LED

Here is the code that uses this approach:

#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "freertos/queue.h"

#define BUTTON_PIN GPIO_NUM_23
#define LED_PIN    GPIO_NUM_2

static QueueHandle_t gpio_evt_queue = NULL;

static void IRAM_ATTR gpio_isr_handler(void* arg) {
    uint32_t gpio_num = (uint32_t) arg;
    xQueueSendFromISR(gpio_evt_queue, &gpio_num, NULL);
}

static void gpio_task(void* arg) {
    uint32_t io_num;
    int led_state = 0;

    while (1) {
        if (xQueueReceive(gpio_evt_queue, &io_num, portMAX_DELAY)) {
            led_state = !led_state;
            gpio_set_level(LED_PIN, led_state);
        }
    }
}

void app_main(void) {
    // Configure LED pin
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_PIN);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_PIN, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    // Configure Button pin with internal pull-up and falling edge interrupt
    gpio_reset_pin(BUTTON_PIN);
    gpio_set_direction(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_MODE_INPUT);
    gpio_set_pull_mode(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_PULLUP_ONLY);
    gpio_set_intr_type(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_INTR_NEGEDGE);

    // Create a queue to handle GPIO events from ISR
    gpio_evt_queue = xQueueCreate(10, sizeof(uint32_t));

    // Start the task to process queue items
    xTaskCreate(gpio_task, "gpio_task", 2048, NULL, 10, NULL);

    // Install GPIO ISR service and add the handler
    gpio_install_isr_service(0);
    gpio_isr_handler_add(BUTTON_PIN, gpio_isr_handler, (void*) BUTTON_PIN);
}

docs.title: Adding debouncing
docs.text:
You might have noticed that the LED flickers when we press the button. This is because the press is almost never clean. We will get multiple hardware interrupts for a single button press, extremely close to each other.

We can ignore those dirty interrupts by checking whether they are too close to the last interrupt.

#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "freertos/queue.h"

#define BUTTON_PIN GPIO_NUM_23
#define LED_PIN    GPIO_NUM_2
#define DEBOUNCE_TIME_MS 50

static QueueHandle_t gpio_evt_queue = NULL;

static void IRAM_ATTR gpio_isr_handler(void* arg) {
    uint32_t gpio_num = (uint32_t) arg;
    xQueueSendFromISR(gpio_evt_queue, &gpio_num, NULL);
}

static void gpio_task(void* arg) {
    uint32_t io_num;
    int led_state = 0;
    TickType_t last_tick = 0;
    const TickType_t debounce_ticks = pdMS_TO_TICKS(DEBOUNCE_TIME_MS);

    while (1) {
        if (xQueueReceive(gpio_evt_queue, &io_num, portMAX_DELAY)) {
            TickType_t current_tick = xTaskGetTickCount();

            // Simple software debounce by checking time elapsed since last valid press
            if ((current_tick - last_tick) > debounce_ticks) {
                last_tick = current_tick;
                led_state = !led_state;
                gpio_set_level(LED_PIN, led_state);
            }
        }
    }
}

void app_main(void) {
    // Configure LED pin
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_PIN);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_PIN, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    // Configure Button pin with internal pull-up and falling edge interrupt
    gpio_reset_pin(BUTTON_PIN);
    gpio_set_direction(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_MODE_INPUT);
    gpio_set_pull_mode(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_PULLUP_ONLY);
    gpio_set_intr_type(BUTTON_PIN, GPIO_INTR_NEGEDGE);

    // Create a queue to handle GPIO events from ISR
    gpio_evt_queue = xQueueCreate(10, sizeof(uint32_t));

    // Start the task to process queue items
    xTaskCreate(gpio_task, "gpio_task", 2048, NULL, 10, NULL);

    // Install GPIO ISR service and add the handler
    gpio_install_isr_service(0);
    gpio_isr_handler_add(BUTTON_PIN, gpio_isr_handler, (void*) BUTTON_PIN);
}

docs.title: Using multiple files
docs.text:
Draft

This chapter is not complete yet.

This is our current project structure (I skipped some files to make it smaller):

.
├── main
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   └── main.c
├── .gitignore
└── CMakeLists.txt

When we built our led_blink project, we put all the code in main.c. But when the project grows, it would be very hard to maintain.

So, what we are going to now, is to define an init_led function and a toggle_led function in a separate file main/led.c, and use them in main.c. But doing this, we can keep main.c shorter & cleaner.

The new project layout will look like this:

.
├── main
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   ├── led.c          <-- New file added
│   └── main.c
├── .gitignore
└── CMakeLists.txt

docs.title: Step 1: Create main/led.c
docs.text:
Paste the following code in led.c file. I am skipping the explanations since we already know this.

#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include <stdbool.h>

#define LED_GPIO_NUM GPIO_NUM_22

// Keep hardware state internal to this file
static bool s_led_on = false;

void led_init(void) {
  gpio_config_t io_conf = {
      .pin_bit_mask = (1ULL << LED_GPIO_NUM),
      .mode = GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT,
      .pull_up_en = GPIO_PULLUP_DISABLE,
      .pull_down_en = GPIO_PULLDOWN_DISABLE,
      .intr_type = GPIO_INTR_DISABLE,
  };
  gpio_config(&io_conf);

  s_led_on = false;
  gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO_NUM, 0);
}

void led_toggle(void) {
  s_led_on = !s_led_on;
  gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO_NUM, s_led_on ? 1 : 0);
}

docs.title: Step 2: Add led.c to main/CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
Your current main/CMakeLists.txt only contains main.c:

idf_component_register(SRCS "main.c"
                    INCLUDE_DIRS ".")

Add led.c in main/CMakeLists.txt (not the root CMakeLists.txt, the one in the main folder):

idf_component_register(SRCS "main.c" "led.c"
                    INCLUDE_DIRS ".")

We'll later cover what idf_component_register means. For now, let's just get this working.

docs.title: Step 3: Add PRIV_REQUIRES to main/CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
Our led.c uses #include "driver/gpio.h". This requires a component named esp_driver_gpio. We will cover what components are later in the course. For now, let's add it:

idf_component_register(SRCS "main.c" "led.c"
                    INCLUDE_DIRS "."
                    PRIV_REQUIRES esp_driver_gpio)

If we are using #include "driver/gpio.h" in main.c, this isn't required. We are required to manually add the components if we use them in other files.

docs.title: Step 4: Update main.c
docs.text:
Now that led.c has been added, you can call the functions in main.c:

#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include <stdio.h>

void app_main(void) {
  led_init(); // from led.c

  while (1) {
    led_toggle(); // from led.c
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(500));
  }
}

docs.title: Step 5: Add declarations in main.c
docs.text:
The compiler compiles each C file separately, and later links them through a process called linking.

Our main.c calls led_init() and led_toggle(). But main.c has no access to led_init() and led_toggle() yet, so it doesn't know how to call those functions (which arguments to pass, what's the return type, etc.). For this, you have to declare the functions before calling them on top of the main file, like this:

#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include <stdio.h>

void led_init(void);    // Declaration for led_init()
void led_toggle(void);  // Declaration for led_toggle()

void app_main(void) {
  led_init();

  while (1) {
    led_toggle();
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(500));
  }
}

Now, when the compiler compiles this file, it leaves placeholders for the address of the functions, which the linker later replace with the actual address. The compiler was able to compile the calling part because we provided the declarations. If we didn't do that, the compiler would not know how to call those functions (whether arguments should be given, what type of arguments, where should the return value go, etc.).

Now, you can test the code.

docs.title: Improving the code
docs.text:
Instead of adding the declarations in main.c, we use something called header files. They have the .h file extension.

Remove the declarations from main.c, and move them to a new file main/led.h. You can add comments on top of the declarations like this:

// Initialize the LED GPIO. Must be called once before led_toggle().
void led_init(void);

// Toggle the LED state (on -> off, off -> on).
void led_toggle(void);

To include these declarations, we use #include "led.h". Update main.c like this:

#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include <stdio.h>
#include "led.h" // New header included

void app_main(void) {
  led_init();

  while (1) {
    led_toggle();
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(500));
  }
}

docs.title: How #include works
docs.text:
Before compiling the code, there is another step called preprocessing. In this step, #include "led.h" is replaced with the contents of led.h.

So, this is functionally similar to putting the declarations in main.c itself. But by separating declarations into a separate file, we can keep main.c cleaner.

Note

Add #pragma once on the very top of the header files to make sure they don't get included multiple times.

docs.title: FAQs
docs.text:
Frequently asked questions:

Can we use #include functions.c in main.c?

Yes, and it works in this case. But it's considered as a bad practice. If we do that, the final file would contain the contents of both main.c and functions.c, which will be large. Even if we only changed functions.c, the entire file will need to be recompiled, which is slow.

docs.title: Mutexes
docs.text: You might have heard this buzzword before. But it's not as complex as it seems. Let me show you exactly what they are by showing a specific situation.

docs.title: Let's create a function: blink_led(int type)
docs.text:
Let's create a function that blinks an LED. It takes a type argument. Type 1 means fast blink, and type 2 means slow blink.

Do not copy the function yet. It's missing headers.

// Define macros for LED blink types
#define BLINK_TYPE_FAST 1
#define BLINK_TYPE_SLOW 2

#define LED_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

void blink_led(int type)
{
    int interval_ms = 0;
    int total_blinks = 0;

    // Configure blink parameters depending on the requested type
    if (type == BLINK_TYPE_FAST)
    {
        // Type 1: Fast blink
        interval_ms = 250;
        total_blinks = 8;
    }
    else if (type == BLINK_TYPE_SLOW)
    {
        // Type 2: Slow blink
        interval_ms = 500;
        total_blinks = 4;
    }
    else
    {
        return;
    }

    // Perform the blinking sequence
    for (int i = 0; i < total_blinks; i++)
    {
        gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 1);
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(interval_ms));
        gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 0);
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(interval_ms));
    }
}

Now assume that this blink function is called by two tasks (Task A and Task B), running in parallel. What will happen?

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
If Task B tries to blink the LED while Task A is blinking the LED, things will mix up and the LED will behave incorrectly.

Now, how do we make Task B wait until Task A stops? So only one task is blinking the LED (calling the blink_led function) at a time?

We can keep a global variable is_blinking, and make it true before starting to blink, and make it false once blinking finishes right?

And ensure is_blinking is false before starting to blink, or wait until it becomes false if it's not, right?

That variable is what we call a mutex. It's technically not a variable (an object), but we'll get to the details soon.

docs.title: Set up the tasks
docs.text:
Let's create Task A and Task B. They do certain kinds of work. But occasionally, they also blink the LED (calls the blink_led() function).

Delete everything in main.c, and define the tasks:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "freertos/semphr.h"
#include "esp_log.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"

// Define macros for LED blink types
#define BLINK_TYPE_FAST 1
#define BLINK_TYPE_SLOW 2

// Define the GPIO pin used for the LED
#define LED_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

// Handle to store our mutex (type: SemaphoreHandle_t)
SemaphoreHandle_t led_mutex = NULL;

void task_a(void *pvParameters)
{
    while (1)
    {
        ESP_LOGI("Task A", "Working (Fast Blink)...");
        // Call the blink_led function
        blink_led(BLINK_TYPE_FAST);
        ESP_LOGI("Task A", "Finished fast blink.");

        ESP_LOGI("Task A", "Doing other tasks.");
        // Mimick work with delay
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100));
    }
}

void task_b(void *pvParameters)
{
    while (1)
    {
        ESP_LOGI("Task B", "Working (Slow Blink)...");
        blink_led(BLINK_TYPE_SLOW);
        ESP_LOGI("Task B", "Finished slow blink.");

        ESP_LOGI("Task B", "Doing other tasks.")
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100));
    }
}

docs.title: Write the main function
docs.text:
Now, create a mutex object and store it in the led_mutex handle. Also start the two tasks, and reset the LED_GPIO.

// ... Existing code ...

void app_main(void)
{
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    // Create the mutex
    led_mutex = xSemaphoreCreateMutex();

    if (led_mutex != NULL)
    {
        // Start both tasks with the same priority (5)
        xTaskCreate(task_a, "Task A", 2048, NULL, 5, NULL);
        xTaskCreate(task_b, "Task B", 2048, NULL, 5, NULL);
    }
    else // When mutex creation fails due to low memory
    {
        ESP_LOGE("APP_MAIN", "Failed to create mutex");
    }
}

docs.title: Function to blink the LED
docs.text:
Now, let's get to the actual part.

We use xSemaphoreTake() to mark the mutex as taken. Like this (do not copy it yet):

xSemaphoreTake(led_mutex, portMAX_DELAY)

Here is the best part: the xSemaphoreTake function doesn't return until it's able to take the mutex. So it waits there indefinitly until the mutex becomes free so it can take it.

While waiting, it consumes zero CPU usage.

Once we are done with the blinking, we can use xSemaphoreGive(led_mutex) to mark the mutex as free again, so other tasks waiting for it to become free will be able to use it.

The second argument tells how long it has to wait. portMAX_DELAY is a macro that means "wait forever". So it won't stop after waiting for a bit.

Here is the blink_led() function:

void blink_led(int type)
{
    int interval_ms = 0;
    int total_blinks = 0;

    if (type == BLINK_TYPE_FAST)
    {
        // Type 1: Fast blink
        interval_ms = 250;
        total_blinks = 8;
    }
    else if (type == BLINK_TYPE_SLOW)
    {
        // Type 2: Slow blink
        interval_ms = 500;
        total_blinks = 4;
    }
    else
    {
        return;
    }

    // Try to take the mutex.
    if (xSemaphoreTake(led_mutex, portMAX_DELAY) == pdTRUE)
    {
        // Perform the blinking sequence
        for (int i = 0; i < total_blinks; i++)
        {
            gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 1);
            vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(interval_ms));
            gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 0);
            vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(interval_ms));
        }

        // Give the mutex back so other tasks can take it
        xSemaphoreGive(led_mutex);
    }
}

Now, blink_led() function ensures that 2 blinks won't happen at the same time. You can now test your code on your ESP32. It should blink slowly and fast alternatively.

docs.title: Full final code
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "freertos/semphr.h"
#include "esp_log.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"

// Define macros for LED blink types
#define BLINK_TYPE_FAST 1
#define BLINK_TYPE_SLOW 2

// Define the GPIO pin used for the LED
#define LED_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

// Declare the mutex handle globally so both tasks can access it
SemaphoreHandle_t led_mutex = NULL;

// Function to blink the LED based on the specified type for 4 seconds
void blink_led(int type)
{
    int interval_ms = 0;
    int total_blinks = 0;

    if (type == BLINK_TYPE_FAST)
    {
        // Type 1: Fast blink
        interval_ms = 250;
        total_blinks = 8;
    }
    else if (type == BLINK_TYPE_SLOW)
    {
        // Type 2: Slow blink
        interval_ms = 500;
        total_blinks = 4;
    }
    else
    {
        return;
    }

    if (xSemaphoreTake(led_mutex, portMAX_DELAY) == pdTRUE)
    {
        // Perform the blinking sequence
        for (int i = 0; i < total_blinks; i++)
        {
            gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 1);
            vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(interval_ms));
            gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 0);
            vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(interval_ms));
        }

        // Give the mutex back so other tasks can take it
        xSemaphoreGive(led_mutex);
    }
}

void task_a(void *pvParameters)
{
    while (1)
    {
        ESP_LOGI("Task A", "Working (Fast Blink)...");
        // Call the blink_led function
        blink_led(BLINK_TYPE_FAST);
        ESP_LOGI("Task A", "Finished fast blink.");

        ESP_LOGI("Task A", "Doing other tasks.");
        // Mimick work with delay
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100));
    }
}

void task_b(void *pvParameters)
{
    while (1)
    {
        ESP_LOGI("Task B", "Working (Slow Blink)...");
        blink_led(BLINK_TYPE_SLOW);
        ESP_LOGI("Task B", "Finished slow blink.");

        ESP_LOGI("Task B", "Doing other tasks.")
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100));
    }
}

void app_main(void)
{
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    // Create the mutex
    led_mutex = xSemaphoreCreateMutex();

    if (led_mutex != NULL)
    {
        // Start both tasks with the same priority (5)
        xTaskCreate(task_a, "Task A", 2048, NULL, 5, NULL);
        xTaskCreate(task_b, "Task B", 2048, NULL, 5, NULL);
    }
    else // When mutex creation fails due to low memory
    {
        ESP_LOGE("APP_MAIN", "Failed to create mutex");
    }
}

docs.title: Hardware required
docs.text:
To complete all chapters in "Basics", you need the following items in addition. All of them are pretty cheap:

  • An LED
  • A 220-330 Ω resistor
  • Jumper wires (M2M, M2F, F2F)

docs.title: Setting up simple circuits using breadboard
docs.text: If you do not know how to set up simple circuits using breadboards, check out this short 3 minute YouTube video (it's easier to learn this way). Skip if you already know how breadboards work.

docs.title: Version control using Git and GitHub
docs.text:
You might already know this. But if you do not, check out this tutorial to learn more.

If everything is set up, let's start!

docs.title: Controlling LED Brightness with PWM
docs.text:
So far, we have only turned our LED fully ON (HIGH voltage) or fully OFF (LOW voltage). But what if you want to set the LED to half brightness, or make it smoothly pulse like a "breathing" light?

Digital pins on the ESP32 can only output either 3.3 V or 0 V. They cannot natively output an intermediate voltage like 1.65 V. To solve this, we use a technique called Pulse Width Modulation (or PWM).

docs.title: What is PWM?
docs.text:
It works by switching the GPIO pin between HIGH and LOW thousands of times per second, far faster than human eyes can notice.

Because the switching happens so quickly, your eyes don't see flickering. Instead, they perceive an average brightness depending on how long the pin remains HIGH during each cycle.

docs.title: Key terminologies
docs.text:
• Duty cycle: The percentage of time the signal stays HIGH during one cycle. For example:
    • 0% duty cycle: The pin is always LOW (LED is OFF).
    • 50% duty cycle: The pin is HIGH for half the time and LOW for half the time (LED appears at half brightness).
    • 100% duty cycle: The pin is always HIGH (LED is at full brightness).
  • Frequency: How many cycles occur per second (measured in Hertz, Hz). For LEDs, a frequency around 5000 Hz (5 kHz) ensures smooth lighting with zero visible flicker.
  • Duty resolution and duty: Used for setting the duty cycle. For example:
    • Setting the duty resolution to 10 bits allows \(2^{10} = 1024\) duty values (from \(0\) to \(1023\)).
    • Setting the duty to 50% of 1023 (approximately 512) makes the brightness 50% (ON from 0 to 511, OFF from 512 to 1023).

docs.title: Other applications of PWM
docs.text:
PWM is not just for dimming LEDs. It is widely used in embedded systems for:

  • Motor speed control: Adjusting the speed of DC motors in fans or electric vehicles.
  • Servo motors: Controlling the precise angle of robotic arms.
  • Buzzer audio: Generating different sound frequencies and tones.

docs.title: The ESP32 LEDC peripheral
docs.text:
The ESP32 includes a dedicated hardware module called LEDC (LED Control). Once you configure it, the LEDC automatically generates the PWM signal in hardware, requiring 0% CPU usage to keep running.

The LEDC peripheral uses two main building blocks:

  1. Timer:
    • Sets the frequency.
    • Sets the duty resolution.
  2. Channel:
    • Sets the duty cycle.
    • Maps the timer signal to a specific physical GPIO pin.

docs.title: Times and channels
docs.text:
The original ESP32 had 8 timers and 16 channels. 4 timers are low speed mode and the other 4 are high speed mode (each numbered from 0 to 4). Newer ESP32 only include low-speed mode timers and channels. So, we always use that.

There is another attribute called hpoint (high point), which is set to 0 by default, meaning the PWM output turns HIGH right at the beginning of the timer cycle (count = 0) and stays HIGH until count == duty.

docs.title: Setup the project
docs.text: Like we did before, create a new project named led_pwm using the sample_project template. Initialize the repository and do the initial commit.

docs.title: Let's write the code!
docs.text:
Let's write a simple program to configure the LEDC peripheral and set our LED to roughly 50% brightness:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "driver/ledc.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"

void app_main(void)
{
    // 1. Configure the LEDC Timer
    ledc_timer_config_t ledc_timer = {
        .speed_mode       = LEDC_LOW_SPEED_MODE, // always
        // You can choose any one of the 4 timers (0, 1, 2, or 3)
        .timer_num        = LEDC_TIMER_0,
        .duty_resolution  = LEDC_TIMER_10_BIT,
        .freq_hz          = 5000,
        // Ignore the following configuration for now
        .clk_cfg          = LEDC_AUTO_CLK
    };
    ledc_timer_config(&ledc_timer);

    // 2. Configure the LEDC Channel
    ledc_channel_config_t ledc_channel = {
        .speed_mode     = LEDC_LOW_SPEED_MODE, // always
        // You can choose any channel
        .channel        = LEDC_CHANNEL_0,
        // Select your timer
        .timer_sel      = LEDC_TIMER_0,
        // Disable interrupts (we don't need them for this)
        .intr_type      = LEDC_INTR_DISABLE,
        // Select your LED GPIO
        .gpio_num       = GPIO_NUM_22,
        .duty           = 0, // Start with LED turned OFF
        // We covered hpoint before
        .hpoint         = 0
    };
    ledc_channel_config(&ledc_channel);

    ESP_LOGI("MAIN", "Setting LED to 50% brightness...");

    // Wait 5 seconds
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(5000));

    // Set duty cycle to ~50% (512 out of 1023)
    ledc_set_duty(LEDC_LOW_SPEED_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL_0, 512);

    // Update duty cycle to apply changes in hardware
    ledc_update_duty(LEDC_LOW_SPEED_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL_0);
}

You can commit your changes whenever you feel you've completed a step. This allows you to experiment with the code and revert to the last completed step if something goes wrong.

docs.title: Improving the code
docs.text:
The standard practice is to define macros for storing configurations on the top of the file. By doing this, you will have all configurations in one place:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "driver/ledc.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"

#define LEDC_GPIO       GPIO_NUM_22
#define LEDC_MODE       LEDC_LOW_SPEED_MODE
#define LEDC_CHANNEL    LEDC_CHANNEL_0
#define LEDC_TIMER      LEDC_TIMER_0
#define LEDC_DUTY_RES   LEDC_TIMER_10_BIT // Resolution: 0 to 1023
#define LEDC_FREQUENCY  5000               // Frequency in Hz (5 kHz)

static const char *TAG = "MAIN";

void app_main(void)
{
    ledc_timer_config_t ledc_timer = {
        .speed_mode       = LEDC_MODE,
        .timer_num        = LEDC_TIMER,
        .duty_resolution  = LEDC_DUTY_RES,
        .freq_hz          = LEDC_FREQUENCY,
        .clk_cfg          = LEDC_AUTO_CLK
    };
    ledc_timer_config(&ledc_timer);

    ledc_channel_config_t ledc_channel = {
        .speed_mode     = LEDC_MODE,
        .channel        = LEDC_CHANNEL,
        .timer_sel      = LEDC_TIMER,
        .intr_type      = LEDC_INTR_DISABLE,
        .gpio_num       = LEDC_GPIO,
        .duty           = 0,
        .hpoint         = 0
    };
    ledc_channel_config(&ledc_channel);

    ESP_LOGI(TAG, "Setting LED to 50%% brightness...");
    vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(5000));

    ledc_set_duty(LEDC_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL, 512);
    ledc_update_duty(LEDC_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL);
}

docs.title: Breathing light effect
docs.text:
Setting a static brightness is a good start, but we can continuously adjust the duty cycle in a loop to create a smooth "breathing" light effect:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "driver/ledc.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"

#define LEDC_GPIO       GPIO_NUM_22
#define LEDC_MODE       LEDC_LOW_SPEED_MODE
#define LEDC_CHANNEL    LEDC_CHANNEL_0
#define LEDC_TIMER      LEDC_TIMER_0
#define LEDC_DUTY_RES   LEDC_TIMER_10_BIT // Duty values range from 0 to 1023
#define LEDC_FREQUENCY  5000               // 5 kHz

void app_main(void)
{
    // Configure Timer
    ledc_timer_config_t ledc_timer = {
        .speed_mode       = LEDC_MODE,
        .timer_num        = LEDC_TIMER,
        .duty_resolution  = LEDC_DUTY_RES,
        .freq_hz          = LEDC_FREQUENCY,
        .clk_cfg          = LEDC_AUTO_CLK
    };
    ledc_timer_config(&ledc_timer);

    // Configure Channel
    ledc_channel_config_t ledc_channel = {
        .speed_mode     = LEDC_MODE,
        .channel        = LEDC_CHANNEL,
        .timer_sel      = LEDC_TIMER,
        .intr_type      = LEDC_INTR_DISABLE,
        .gpio_num       = LEDC_GPIO,
        .duty           = 0,
        .hpoint         = 0
    };
    ledc_channel_config(&ledc_channel);

    while (1) {
        // Fade in: gradually increase duty cycle from 0 to 1023
        for (int duty = 0; duty <= 1023; duty += 15) {
            ledc_set_duty(LEDC_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL, duty);
            ledc_update_duty(LEDC_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL);
            vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(15));
        }

        // Fade out: gradually decrease duty cycle from 1023 down to 0
        for (int duty = 1023; duty >= 0; duty -= 15) {
            ledc_set_duty(LEDC_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL, duty);
            ledc_update_duty(LEDC_MODE, LEDC_CHANNEL);
            vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(15));
        }
    }
}

Build and flash this code to see your LED smoothly pulsing!

docs.title: Test your knowledge
docs.text:
Try answering the questions below:

What is the difference between duty cycle and duty?

Duty cycle is the percentage of time the signal stays HIGH. Duty is the numerical value you configure to control that percentage (more about duty above).

What are the roles of the Timer and Channel inside the ESP32's LEDC peripheral?

If the timer resolution is configured to 8-bit (LEDC_TIMER_8_BIT), what duty value corresponds to 100% brightness?

For an 8-bit timer resolution (\(2^8 = 256\)), the duty values range from 0 to 255. So, 255 corresponds to 100% brightness.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Let's upgrade our blink LED code. Instead of blinking the LED directly inside app_main(), let's create a function blink_led() and call it from app_main():

#include <stdio.h>
#include "freertos/FreeRTOS.h"
#include "freertos/task.h"
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"

#define LED_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

// More on `void *pvParameter` later (hang tight)
void blink_led(void *pvParameter) {
    while (1) {
        gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 1);
        ESP_LOGI("LED", "LED State: ON");
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));

        gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, 0);
        ESP_LOGI("LED", "LED State: OFF");
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(1000));
    }
}

void app_main(void) {
    gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
    gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

    blink_led();
}

Now, imagine we need to log "LED started blinking" after calling blink_led(). But this is not possible because blink_led() runs an infinite loop and doesn't return.

Even if we add ESP_LOGI("LED", "LED started blinking") after blink_led() call, it won't reach there.

docs.title: The fix
docs.text:
Instead of calling blink_led() directly, what if we let it run parallel to app_main()? app_main() only need to start blink_led(). It will run on it's own from then, and app_main() can do other stuff.

To do this, we create a Task using the blink_led() function. Once we create a task, it starts running parallel to app_main().

We can use the xTaskCreate() function to create tasks. Update app_main() like this:

void app_main(void) {
  gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
  gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

  // Create the task
  xTaskCreate(blink_led,    // The task function
              "blink_task", // Name of the task (used for debugging)
              2048,         // RAM allocated to the task (in bytes)
              NULL,         // Pointer to the parameters passed to the task function blink_led (NULL since we aren't giving any parameters)
              1,            // Priority of the task (we'll discuss this later)
              NULL          // Task handle to track or control the task later (we aren't using this as of now, so NULL)
  );

  // Now you can do anything else here.
  // Let's log something!
  ESP_LOGI("LED", "LED started blinking");
}

Now you can test your code & ensure it's working.

docs.title: A few improvements
docs.text: Since blink_led() is a task, it's better to rename it to blink_led_task() or blink_task(). But it's optional.

docs.title: Task priority
docs.text:
In bigger firmware, we might have multiple tasks running in parallel. In those cases, task priority matters a lot.

Here are the key points:

  • Task priority is a number assigned to a task that represents the priority of the task.
  • Higher priority tasks block lower priority tasks. Lower priority tasks can only execute if higher priority tasks stop (temporarily or permanently).
  • If both tasks have the same priority, they run in parallel.

We will be creating programs with multiple tasks later in the course!

docs.title: Timers
docs.text: This time, we are going to blink an LED using a timer.

docs.title: Timers and callback functions
docs.text:
A timer allows us to schedule an action to happen (a function to be called) after a specified amount of time.

The function we give to the timer is called callback function. The timer will call it after the specified amount of time. Callback functions aren't some new kind of functions, they are called so because of their purpose.

docs.title: Types of timers
docs.text:
There are two common types of timers:

  • One-shot timer: Invokes its callback once after the specified interval and then stops.
  • Periodic timer: Invokes its callback repeatedly at the specified interval until it is manually stopped.

For example, assume we give flash_led() function as the timer callback. If we start a one-shot timer with a duration of 1 seconds, the LED flashes after 1 second. But if we use a periodic timer, the LED flashes after 1 second, 2 seconds, 3 seconds, and so on.

docs.title: The esp_timer API
docs.text:
ESP-IDF provides the esp_timer.h for creating software timers.

Here are some of it's important functions. You don't have to memorize these. The names are self-explanatory.

Function Purpose esp_timer_create() Create a timer esp_timer_start_once() Start a one-shot timer esp_timer_start_periodic() Start a periodic timer esp_timer_stop() Stop a running timer esp_timer_restart() Restart an active timer with a new timeout esp_timer_delete() Delete a timer

We will use esp_timer_create() and esp_timer_start_once() in this project.

docs.title: Are timers reliable?
docs.text: Software timers do not guarantee perfectly exact callback execution times. System load and callback scheduling can introduce delays.

docs.title: Set up the project
docs.text: Create a new empty project using the sample_project template, as covered in Your First Project. Name it led_timer.

docs.title: Setup the circuit
docs.text:
We will use GPIO22 for the LED and GPIO23 for the button, just like in our previous chapters. The circuit is also same as before:

  • Connect the positive terminal of the LED to GPIO22.
  • Connect the negative terminal to a 220–330 Ω resistor.
  • Connect the other end of the resistor to GND.

docs.title: What we are going to do
docs.text:
1. Create a toggle_led function.
  2. Create a timer with toggle_led as the callback.
  3. Start the timer as a periodic timer with a period of 1 second.

The timer will call toggle_led() every second.

docs.title: Write the code
docs.text:
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"
#include "esp_timer.h"

#define LED_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

static const char *TAG = "MAIN";
static bool led_state = false;

// The function to be called every time the timer fires
static void toggle_led(void *arg) {
  led_state = !led_state;
  gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, led_state);
  ESP_LOGI(TAG, "LED toggled to: %d", led_state);
}

void app_main(void) {
  gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
  gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

  // Set up the timer creation arguments
  const esp_timer_create_args_t timer_args = {
      .callback = &toggle_led,   // Called when the timer expires
      .name = "toggle_led_timer" // For debugging purposes only
  };

  // Handle to store the timer instance
  esp_timer_handle_t led_timer;

  // Create the timer instance using timer_args
  esp_timer_create(&timer_args, &led_timer);

  // Start the timer in periodic mode with a 1-second interval (1,000,000
  // microseconds)
  esp_timer_start_periodic(led_timer, 1000000);
}

docs.title: Improving the code
docs.text:
ESP-IDF provides a function-like macro ESP_ERROR_CHECK(). Here is how it works:

we wrap a function inside ESP_ERROR_CHECK, like this:

ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_timer_create())

If esp_timer_create() fails, it returns a non-zero return code (this behaviour is coded to the esp_timer_create() function itself, as well as many other ESP-IDF functions). If that happens, ESP_ERROR_CHECK function returns an error, ESP-IDF logs the error and aborts the program.

If we do not use it, and an error occurs, the firmware continues running. We will never know about the error, and it would be really painful to troubleshoot later.

Wrap esp_timer_create() and esp_timer_start_periodic() inside ESP_ERROR_CHECK() to improve the code.

docs.title: Final full code
docs.text:
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "esp_log.h"
#include "esp_timer.h"

#define LED_GPIO GPIO_NUM_22

static const char *TAG = "MAIN";
static bool led_state = false;

// The function to be called every time the timer fires
static void toggle_led(void *arg) {
  led_state = !led_state;
  gpio_set_level(LED_GPIO, led_state);
  ESP_LOGI(TAG, "LED toggled to: %d", led_state);
}

void app_main(void) {
  gpio_reset_pin(LED_GPIO);
  gpio_set_direction(LED_GPIO, GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT);

  // Set up the timer creation arguments
  const esp_timer_create_args_t timer_args = {
      .callback = &toggle_led,   // Called when the timer expires
      .name = "toggle_led_timer" // For debugging purposes only
  };

  // Handle to store the timer instance
  esp_timer_handle_t led_timer;

  // Create the timer instance using timer_args
  ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_timer_create(&timer_args, &led_timer));

  // Start the timer in periodic mode with a 1-second interval (1,000,000
  // microseconds)
  ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_timer_start_periodic(led_timer, 1000000));
}

Now, you can test the project and ensure it's working.

docs.title: Your first project
docs.text:
Hardware required:

  • An ESP32 microcontroller.
  • A suitable cable to connect it to your PC.

docs.title: Create a new empty project
docs.text:
We are going to use the ESP-IDF: New Project command from the command palette to create the project.

  • Open the command palette using Ctrl + Shift + P.
  • Search for and click on ESP-IDF: New Project, and wait.
  • Select your ESP-IDF version (you might see only one version since we only installed one), and wait.
  • A new tab will pop up. Inside that tab, under ESP-IDF Templates, select the sample_project template and click the "Create Project" button.

The tab will refresh, and you will see a form to fill in your project details. Fill in the details:

  • Project name: Your project name.
  • Project directory: Your project directory.
  • ESP-IDF target: esp32.
  • ESP-IDF board: Custom board.
  • Serial port: Detect.
  • OpenOCD configuration files: Keep the default value.
  • ESP-IDF component directory: Keep the input empty.

Click "Create Project" and wait again. After creation, in the new tab that pops up, click "Open Project". This will open your brand new ESP-IDF project in a fresh VS Code window.

docs.title: Install an Extension for Intellisense
docs.text: We need an extension for proper syntax highlighting and text suggestions.

docs.title: Option 1: Microsoft C/C++ extension (easiest to set up)
docs.text: Install the extensions from the "Extensions" tab. That's it.

docs.title: Option 2: Clangd (if you are using a VS Code fork)
docs.text: Install Clangd from the "Extensions" tab. Then, run ESP-IDF: Configure project for ESP-Clang from the VS Code command palette.

docs.title: Whatever you choose...
docs.text:
Note

You have to make sure both of them aren't activated at the same time, as they can interfere with each other.

docs.title: Configure your project
docs.text:
You need to configure your project whenever you:

  • Start a new project (like we did now)
  • Add, remove, or rename source code files
  • Include new headers (e.g., #include esp_log.h)
  • And so on.

But it's safe to do again and again. Since we just created a new project, let's run it by clicking the ESP-IDF: Run idf.py reconfigure Task command from the command palette.

This will take some time. While it's working, let's learn what it does:

  • Generates (or regenerates) the build files in the build folder
  • Generates compile_commands.json, which is essential for Microsoft C/C++ Extension or Clangd to provide IntelliSense
  • And a lot more (just know these two for now)

Troubleshooting tip

Sometimes, error squiggles appear even though your code is completely correct. This typically happens when your compile_commands.json file is outdated and hasn't synced with your latest changes.

To resolve this, run the ESP-IDF: Run idf.py reconfigure Task command from the command palette to refresh your project configuration and clear out the false warnings.

docs.title: Let's write some code
docs.text:
If you look at main.c right now, you will see an empty main function (app_main):

#include <stdio.h>

void app_main(void)
{

}

Let's log "Hello world!" inside it.

docs.title: Hello, world!
docs.text:
We use a function called ESP_LOGI() to log "Hello world!" (I stands for "info"). Include the esp_log.h header to use that function. The function takes two arguments: a TAG, and the actual string to log.

#include "esp_log.h"

void app_main(void) {
  ESP_LOGI("MAIN", "Hello world!");
}

This code will log something like this:

I (312) MAIN: Hello world!

Here,

  • I: Log level indicator (Info).
  • (312): Timestamp in milliseconds since boot (this exact number will vary).
  • MAIN: Tag name (useful to determine the source of the LOG message when we have a lot of them).
  • Hello world!: The actual content.

docs.title: Building (compiling) the project
docs.text:
Open the command palette (Ctrl + Shift + P) and run

ESP-IDF: Build Your Project

This will also take some time. Be patient.

docs.title: Flashing your project
docs.text:
Flashing is like uploading the compiled code to your ESP32. You need to physically connect the ESP32 to your computer. After doing that, run the following command from the command palette:

ESP-IDF: Flash (UART) Your Project

It probably won't work out of the box. The fix differs depending on your platform.

docs.title: If you are using Windows
docs.text:
If you are on Windows, flashing might show this error:

A fatal error occurred: Could not connect to an Espressif device on any of the 1 available serial ports.

If that happens, the next time you try, press and hold the BOOT button on your board as soon as you see Connecting.... You can release when the Connecting... stops and you see other outputs. Once flash is finished, you will see this:

Flash Done ⚡️
Flash has finished. You can monitor your device with 'ESP-IDF: Monitor Device'

docs.title: If you are using Linux (e.g., Ubuntu)
docs.text:
You might get this error while flashing:

A fatal error occurred: Could not open /dev/ttyUSB0, the port is busy or doesn't exist.
([Errno 13] could not open port /dev/ttyUSB0: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/dev/ttyUSB0')

Hint: Try to add the user to the dialout or uucp group.

If that happens, run this command, log out, log back in (or reboot), and try flashing again:

sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER

If the flash succeeds, you will get this:

Flash Done ⚡️
Flash has finished. You can monitor your device with 'ESP-IDF: Monitor Device'

You have to do it only once per system. Subsequent flashing will work without running this command.

docs.title: Monitoring the device
docs.text:
You should keep your ESP32 connected to your computer so that it receives power and is running. Let's check whether the "Hello world!" got logged.

At the bottom of VS Code, you will see several icons. Find the icon that looks like a monitor and hover over it. If you see "Monitor Device" when you hover, you found the correct icon.

Click on that icon. You will see several logs popping up. These are sent internally. But among those log messages, you will find our Hello world:

I (258) main_task: Started on CPU0
I (258) main_task: Calling app_main()
I (258) MAIN: Hello world!   <--------------- this
I (258) main_task: Returned from app_main()

You might see different numbers than 258. That's not a problem.

So, congratulations! You just set up your computer for ESP-IDF, created a new project, wrote some code, compiled, flashed, and monitored the output!

docs.title: Adding the VS Code Configuration Folder
docs.text: If you accidentally deleted/edited the .vscode folder, you can regenerate it using the ESP-IDF: Add VS Code Configuration Folder command from the command palette.

docs.title: Test Your Knowledge
docs.text:
Test your knowledge by answering the following questions:

  • How do we create a new ESP-IDF project? Which template should we use for an empty project?
  • When do we need to configure our project? How can we do it? Is it safe to do it repeatedly?
  • How to build, flash, and monitor.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
We have to install 2 things:

  1. ESP-IDF: The framework we use for programming our ESP32.
  2. ESP-IDF VS Code Extension: To interact with ESP-IDF.

docs.title: Install ESP-IDF
docs.text: Espressif Systems provides a graphical tool called EIM (ESP-IDF Installation Manager) to install ESP-IDF. We have to install EIM first.

docs.title: Install EIM
docs.text:
Click the link below to go to the official page to download EIM:

https://dl.espressif.com/dl/eim/

Make sure you are in the "Online Installer" tab. The exact file to download depends on your system:

  • Windows: Download eim-gui-windows-x64.exe. Run this installer to install EIM.
  • Linux x64 (Ubuntu): Download and install the .deb package (eim-gui-linux-x64.deb).

docs.title: Install ESP-IDF using EIM
docs.text:
Now that we have installed EIM, let's install ESP-IDF using it.

  1. Open EIM.
  2. Under "New Installation" click "Start Installation".
  3. Under "Easy Installation", click "Start Easy Installation" to install the latest stable version of ESP-IDF with default settings.
  4. If there are no problems, you will see the "Ready to Install" page. Click "Start Installation".

docs.title: Install ESP-IDF VS Code Extension
docs.text:
We use this extension as a high-level wrapper for ESP-IDF. Most times, we do not use ESP-IDF directly. For example, if we need to compile our source code, we ask the extension to do it, which uses the ESP-IDF we just installed internally to to compile the source code.

Install the extension named "ESP-IDF" by "Espressif Systems" in VS Code.

After installing, restart VS Code. You might get this notification:

No standard ESP-IDF project was found in this workspace. Do you want to activate the ESP-IDF extension anyway?

Click "Activate Anyway". This will activate the extension.

docs.title: Verify installation
docs.text: Use the shortcut Ctrl + Shift + P to open the command palette (remember this shortcut, we are going to use it a lot). Inside the command palette, search ESP-IDF. You will see many entries which start with ESP-IDF:. Those commands are provided my the ESP-IDF extension. These commands are what we use for almost everything.

docs.title: Test your knowledge
docs.text:
Each chapter ends with this section. The purpose is to solidify important things that you might need frequently in your memory using active recall.

How do we open the command palette?

Using the shortcut Ctrl + Shift + P.
